templates.scenario: At {workplace|the}, your {lead} points out that you have been skipping a step in {task|the}. You feel a little defensive because you thought you were doing it well.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Thank your {lead}, ask for an example of the missed step, and adjust how you do the task.
options.why: Accepting feedback and asking for specifics shows you are open to improving, and it makes the change easier to carry out.

options.text: Explain why you skip the step so that your {lead} understands you were not being careless.
options.why: Context can help, but leading with an explanation sounds defensive and misses the chance to learn what your {lead} saw.
options.misconception: Explaining my reasons is the best way to respond to feedback.

options.text: Say you will do better, but keep doing the task exactly as before since it seems to work.
options.why: Agreeing without changing anything means the feedback was ignored, and the same issue will come up again.
options.misconception: Agreeing politely is the same as acting on feedback.

options.text: Ask several coworkers whether they think the step really matters, before deciding what to do about it.
options.why: Seeking support for your view turns feedback into a vote. The person who asked for the change is the best source for why it matters.
options.misconception: Feedback is optional if others disagree with it.

templates.principle: Accept feedback by thanking the person, asking for specifics, and making a real change.

templates.scenario: An update to {system|the} at {workplace|the} changes how you do your daily tasks. Training is scheduled for next week, but you have to use the updated version tomorrow. A quick-start guide is posted, and {coworker} has already used the new version.

options.text: Read the quick-start guide and ask {coworker} about the key changes, and still attend next week's training.
options.why: Using the guide and an experienced coworker gets you working now, and the scheduled training fills in the rest.

options.text: Wait for next week's training before using any of the new features, and ask someone else to handle tasks until then.
options.why: Waiting leaves your work to others and delays your learning. Resources were available to start right away.
options.misconception: Training is the only real way to learn something new.

options.text: Click around in the updated version to see what happens, since learning by trial is quickest.
options.why: Trying things at random may cause mistakes in real work. A guide and an experienced coworker are faster and safer.
options.misconception: Experimenting alone is the most efficient way to learn.

options.text: Keep using your old way of working for as long as possible, until someone makes you switch.
options.why: Resisting change builds a gap that gets harder to close, and the update is going to be used tomorrow regardless.
options.misconception: If I ignore a change, it may go away.

templates.principle: When a change arrives before formal training, use guides and experienced coworkers right away, then add training.
templates.timing: Use is required tomorrow, so informal resources come before the scheduled training.

templates.scenario: {Workplace|the} announces a new procedure for {task|the} that replaces the method you have used for years. It is required for everyone starting next week. You believe the old method was faster.

options.text: Learn the new procedure, use it as required, and share specific observations with your {lead} after a fair trial.
options.why: A fair trial gives real evidence. Specific, constructive observations are more useful than a first reaction.

options.text: Use the new procedure and tell your {lead} right away that you think it will be slower.
options.why: Following the procedure is right, but voicing a conclusion before trying it is less persuasive than feedback based on experience.
options.misconception: My first impression is the most useful input.

options.text: Keep using the old method quietly when no one is checking, since it gets the same results faster.
options.why: The procedure is required for everyone. Using a different method on your own can cause inconsistency and may hide a concern that could help the team.
options.misconception: Results matter more than following the new process.

options.text: Tell coworkers the change is a mistake and encourage them to share their doubts about it as well.
options.why: Venting spreads resistance without giving decision-makers any useful information. Constructive feedback does more to improve the procedure.
options.misconception: If many people complain, the change will be reversed.

templates.principle: Adapt to required changes by learning them well, giving them a fair trial, and then offering specific feedback.

review.notes: Requirement stated; acceptable option is cooperative but premature.

templates.scenario: {coworker} writes this note while planning a move into a new role at {workplace|the}.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that is a problem.

segments.text: I want to move into the new technician role next year.
segments.whyFine: Stating a goal clearly is a good start.

segments.text: The job posting lists a safety certification as required.
segments.whyFine: This simply records a fact from the posting.

segments.text: I will skip the certification and apply anyway, since it probably does not matter.
segments.why: A listed requirement matters. Skipping it without checking can mean not being considered, and earning it would strengthen the application.

segments.text: I will ask my supervisor how to prepare for the next steps.
segments.whyFine: Asking for guidance on preparation is a sensible step.

templates.principle: When a role lists a credential as required, plan to earn it instead of assuming it does not matter.

review.notes: Only one line disregards a stated requirement.

templates.scenario: A new skill is becoming important in jobs at {workplace|the}, and you want to learn it.
templates.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Identify the skill you need to build
Find a reliable resource or someone who can teach it
Use the skill on the job and keep improving

precedence.why: You need to know the skill before you can find a way to learn it.
You need something reliable to practice from.
Practice with feedback prepares you to use the skill on real work.

templates.principle: Learn a new skill by naming it, finding a good resource, practicing with feedback, and then applying it.
